paper.title: School Absence Among Children With Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis: A National Matched Comparison Study
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement. Ethics: 'The study was approved by the Danish Data Protection Agency through the Aarhus University comment agreement (journal no. …

registers.name_in_paper: STIL (the Danish Agency for Information, Technology, and Learning), stil.dk
variables_mentioned: days absent per potential school days

registers.role: covariates: socioeconomic status and sex; sample frame

registers.name_in_paper: the CPR number (unique social security number given to every resident in Denmark)

registers.role: data source named in the Setting section

linkages: Registers linked at the individual level through the CPR number assigned to every resident in Denmark
Children with JIA linked to 5 reference children per case, matched on school, grade level, school year and sex
School absence registrations (STIL) linked to hospital diagnoses (DNPR) and to Statistics Denmark SES data

sample.universe: All children born in Denmark after December 31, 1994 who attended Danish public schools between the school years 2010/11 and 2018/19
sample.unit_of_observation: child; school absence aggregated to the child-year (or child-month in the monthly analysis) relative to the index month
selection_rules: Children with >= 5 ICD-10 diagnostic codes for JIA (DM08 or DM09) in the DNPR are classified as exposed
Index date is the first hospital visit (inpatient or outpatient) with a JIA diagnosis code
Each child with JIA matched to 5 reference children with no JIA diagnosis at time of matching who had school absence data available, matched on school, grade level, school year and sex
Primary study: children diagnosed with JIA after starting school; index month = month of the first registered JIA diagnosis (children diagnosed in July matched in August of the same year)
Secondary study: children whose first JIA contact was before starting school; index month = month they started school
Primary study: only children with >= 5 months of school absence registrations in the year before or after the index month are included
Secondary study: only children with >= 5 months of school absence registrations in grade 0 are included
To enter the analysis of a specific time period a child had to have >= 5 months of absence registrations for the yearly analyses, or >= 5 days for the monthly analyses
Complete case analysis for the adjusted analyses
sample.period: school years 2010/11 to 2018/19 (children diagnosed between 2010 and 2019)
sample.n_individuals: 786 children with JIA and 3908 matched controls in the primary study; 382 children with JIA and 1910 matched controls in the secondary study

construction_notes: School absence is registered daily for each pupil in all public schools in Denmark and reported by calendar month; it enters the study as days absent per potential school days for the specific child
Total absence is the sum of sickness, legal and illegal absence
Problematic school absence is nonlegal (sickness and illegal) absence of > 10%, dichotomized as 1 = >= 10%; 0 = < 10%

Family income divided into 3 groups corresponding to the tertile of family income of all children born between 1995 and 2018 in the calendar year of diagnosis or matching; incomes of 0 Danish kroner or less reported as missing
Parental educational level = highest educational level of the parents the year before the index month, grouped by UNESCO ISCED into short (1-2), medium (3-5) and long (6-8)
Family structure dichotomized into living with a single caretaker vs not
All SES variables taken from the year before the index month; if unavailable, from the index year
Values below 5 cannot be reported according to the rules of Statistics Denmark
Mean age at diagnosis 11.3 years (SD 2.9) in the primary study and 3.2 years in the secondary study

claims.statement: Among children diagnosed with JIA after starting school, the total school absence rate in the fifth year before diagnosis was not statistically distinguishable from that of matched schoolmates without JIA (adjusted IRR 1).

register_source.value: DNPR (Danish National Patient Register): ICD-10 diagnosis codes DM08 or DM09, >= 5 codes

definition.value: Binary exposure: children with >= 5 ICD-10 diagnostic codes for JIA (DM08 or DM09) in the Danish National Patient Register are classified as exposed; the index date is the first hospital visit (inpatient or outpatient) with a JIA diagnosis code. Comparison group: matched schoolmates with no JIA diagnosis at the time of matching.

timing.value: Measured at the index month = month of the first registered JIA diagnosis (first inpatient or outpatient hospital contact with a JIA code), which occurs after the child has started school

register_source.value: STIL (Danish Agency for Information, Technology, and Learning): daily school absence registrations for pupils in Danish public schools, reported by calendar month, school years 2010/11-2018/19

definition.value: Total school absence: days absent per potential school days for the specific child; total absence is the sum of sickness, legal and illegal absence. School absence is registered daily for each pupil in all public schools in Denmark and reported by calendar month; expressed here as the mean absence percentage over the period.

timing.value: Mean total school absence rate measured over the fifth year before diagnosis (index month = month of the first registered JIA diagnosis or of matching)

units.value: incidence rate ratio: school absence rate of children with JIA relative to matched children without JIA

estimand.target_population: children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis attending Danish public schools, relative to matched schoolmates without JIA
estimand.formal_query: adjusted rate ratio E[Y | JIA = 1, X] / E[Y | JIA = 0, X] (X = matching and adjustment variables); the paper reports it as an association, not as a do-expression

population.description: Children born in Denmark after December 31, 1994 who attended Danish public schools in the school years 2010/11-2018/19 and were diagnosed with JIA after starting school (786 children), together with 3908 matched schoolmates without JIA
subgroups_defined: sex
parental educational level (short / medium / long, ISCED)
family income (low / medium / high tertile)
family structure (living with a single caretaker vs not)
population.selection: Attending a Danish public school with school absence registrations; matched 1:5 to schoolmates on school, grade level, school year and sex; only children with >= 5 months of absence registrations in the year before or after the index month enter the yearly analyses; adjusted analyses are complete-case

identification.source_of_variation: Matched cohort design on Danish register data: each child with JIA is matched to 5 reference children without a JIA diagnosis at the time of matching, matched on school, grade level, school year and sex, and school absence rates are compared between the two groups in each period relative to the index month. There is no reform, lottery or discontinuity - the comparison rests on matching plus covariate adjustment.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the matching variables (school, grade level, school year, sex) and on the adjustment set (sex, age at diagnosis or matching, parental educational level, family income, family structure), JIA status is independent of the potential school absence outcomes - i.e. children with and without JIA are otherwise comparable
key_assumptions.supported_by: Matching on school, grade level, school year and sex; adjustment for sex, age, parental education, family income and family structure; Table 1 reports no significant differences in the distribution of SES variables between children with JIA and peers without JIA

rhs: potential school absence outcomes Y(JIA=1), Y(JIA=0)

key_assumptions.assumption: Misclassification of JIA status induced by requiring >= 5 JIA diagnostic codes is nondifferential: it is unrelated to school absence
key_assumptions.supported_by: The authors argue that excluding children with fewer than 5 diagnosis codes gives undifferentiated misclassification because it is not related to the outcome

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysis sample is conditioned on attending a Danish public school and on having at least 5 months of school absence registrations in the relevant period (and, for the adjusted estimates, on complete covariate data); the comparison is assumed to be undistorted by this conditioning
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated inclusion rules; the authors note that approximately 85% of all children in Denmark attend public schools

implies_edges.from: availability of >= 5 months of school absence registrations

threats_discussed: Misclassification of JIA status from the requirement of >= 5 diagnostic codes
No information on type of JIA or disease status, so SA cannot be related to disease type or activity
No information on absence before school start (kindergarten) for children diagnosed very young
Only children in public schools are observed (approximately 85% of Danish children)
The cause of the recorded sickness absence and of the legal absence is unknown
robustness_checks: Subgroup analyses stratified on sex, parental educational level, family income and family structure (Supplementary Figures S1A-D and S2A-D, available from the authors on request)
Separate analyses of problematic school absence (> 10% nonlegal absence), Figures 3 and 5
Monthly school absence rates from 24 months before to 24 months after the index month (Figure 2)
Complete case analysis for the adjusted analyses
unresolved_confounders: Type of JIA and disease status could not be included or evaluated
The cause of the sickness absence is unknown
The cause of the legal school absence is unknown

estimator.value: Adjusted negative binomial regression reporting incidence rate ratios (IRRs)

estimation.specification: Adjusted negative binomial regression of school absence (days absent per potential school days) on an indicator for JIA, adjusted for sex, family income level, parental educational level, family structure and age at diagnosis, estimated separately for each year relative to the index month and for each type of absence; the paper prints no estimating equation.

sample_n.value: 113 children with JIA and 571 children without JIA

source_table.value: Figure 1, Fifth year before diagnosis block, 'Total school absence' row (adjusted IRR with 95% CI)

heterogeneity.dimension: socioeconomic status (family income, parental educational level, family structure)
heterogeneity.finding: Both children with and without JIA from families with lower income, shorter parental educational level and single-caretaker households had higher rates of school absence, but neither SES nor sex modified the JIA-absence rate ratio (Supplementary Figures S1A-D / 2A-D, available from the authors on request)

heterogeneity.dimension: sex
heterogeneity.finding: Sex did not modify the association between JIA and school absence measured as IRR

nodes: availability of >= 5 months of school absence registrations

edges.from: availability of >= 5 months of school absence registrations

evidence.annotation: Figure 1. School absence rates of children with and without JIA in children diagnosed after starting school (primary study). Adjusted IRRs are based on adjusted negative binomial regressions. Adjusted for sex, family income level, parental educational level, family structure, and age at diagnosis. IRR estimates > 1 indicate higher rates of school absence among children with JIA. IRR estimates < 1 indicate higher school absence rates among controls. IRR: incidence rate ratio; JIA: juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

value.claimed_domain: countries following similar JIA treatment protocols and with similar school systems
boundary_conditions: patients treated in accordance with the Danish JIA treatment protocol, which follows American College of Rheumatology and PReS/EULAR guidelines
all primary-study patients and most secondary-study patients were diagnosed after the introduction of biologic treatment
a school system in which absence is registered as in Danish public schools
